extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs, logic, and elementary combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for negating logical statements, basic rules of inference, and elementary counting principles (multiplication, addition, subtraction, factorials/permutations) used in writing and understanding proofs and solving counting problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of a conjunction (DeMorgan style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation of a conjunction (P ∧ Q) is equivalent to the disjunction of the negations: ∼(P ∧ Q) = ∼P ∨ ∼Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The numbers x and y are both odd' ( (x odd) ∧ (y odd) ) negates to '(x is even) ∨ (y is even)'. Use this when translating everyday language into precise logical negations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Negating quantified statements flips the quantifier and negates the predicate: ∼(∀ x ∈ X, P(x)) = ∃ x ∈ X, ∼P(x) and ∼(∃ x ∈ X, P(x)) = ∀ x ∈ X, ∼P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read in words: 'It is not the case that P(x) is true for all x' means 'There exists an x for which P(x) is false.' Use these equivalences repeatedly when negating statements with quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of implication
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation of a conditional P ⇒ Q is equivalent to P ∧ ∼Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the truth table, the only way P ⇒ Q is false is when P is true and Q is false. Example: negating 'If a is odd, then a^2 is odd' gives 'a is odd and a^2 is not odd.' For universally quantified conditionals, apply quantifier-negation rules first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating statements with multiple quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the quantifier-negation rule iteratively, flipping quantifiers and negating predicates in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Negating S: '∀ x ∈ R, ∃ y ∈ R, y^3 = x' gives '∃ x ∈ R, ∀ y ∈ R, y^3 ≠ x'. Work from the outermost quantifier inward, flipping each as you negate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal logical symbols to disambiguate mathematical sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate everyday mathematical language into symbols (∧, ∨, ⇒, ⇔, ∼, ∀, ∃) to pin down exact meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that logic gives exact meanings to words like 'and', 'or', 'not', 'if... then', and that parsing sentences with these symbols (mentally or on scratch paper) helps avoid ambiguity when reading or writing mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens (rule of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: From P ⇒ Q and P, infer Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fundamental pattern used constantly in proofs. Represented diagrammatically with the premises above a line and the conclusion below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus tollens (rule of inference)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify via truth tables if needed; commonly used to deduce the falsity of antecedents from falsity of consequents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunctive syllogism / Elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: From P ∨ Q and ∼P, infer Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named 'Elimination' in the text; an intuitively obvious but frequently used inference pattern in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction introduction and elimination; disjunction introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are true then P ∧ Q is true; if P ∧ Q is true then P (and Q) is true; if P is true then P ∨ Q is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are basic obvious inferences the text lists for routine use in proofs—be aware you are using these patterns when combining or breaking down statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a list (ordered sequence) and strings
rubrics_metrics.description: A list is an ordered sequence of objects, denoted (a, b, c, ...); order matters and repeats are allowed. A string is a list written without parentheses/commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two lists are equal only if same entries in same positions. The empty list ( ) has length zero. Beware that omitting parentheses can create ambiguity (e.g., '9 10 11' vs '9,10,11').

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle (Fundamental Counting Principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If making a list of length n has a1 choices for the first entry, a2 for the second, ..., an for the nth, then the total number of different lists is a1 · a2 · ... · an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tree diagrams to visualize but compute by multiplication. Examples: license plates (26^3 · 10^4), café order choices (3·3·2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling repetition vs non-repetition in counting
rubrics_metrics.description: When repetition is allowed, each position has the same number of choices; when repetition is not allowed, available choices decrease as positions are filled (n, n-1, n-2,...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: non-repetitive lists of length 4 from 4 letters: 4·3·2·1 = 24. Be careful to account for depletion of options when repetition is forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition Principle (summing disjoint cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a finite set X is decomposed as a disjoint union X = X1 ∪ X2 ∪ ... ∪ Xn (Xi ∩ Xj = ∅ for i≠j), then |X| = |X1| + |X2| + ... + |Xn|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to break a counting problem into mutually exclusive cases (e.g., categorize by position of a distinguished element). Ensure cases are disjoint to avoid double-counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting when partitioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing into types/cases, ensure each element belongs to exactly one case; otherwise elements may be counted multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example pitfall: counting lists containing an E by summing counts for E-in-first + E-in-second + ... overcounts lists with multiple E's. Use disjoint partitioning or inclusion-exclusion as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction Principle (count complement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊆ U for finite sets, then |U − X| = |U| − |X|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when it's easier to count the complement. Example: number of lists with at least one E = total lists − lists with no E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: fill restricted positions first under non-repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: When positional constraints interact with non-repetition, assign values to the restricted positions first to avoid ambiguity about available choices later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: counting non-repetitive lists where first must be from {B,C,D} and last must be a vowel—fill first and last, then fill middle positions from remaining letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial and permutations (n!)
rubrics_metrics.description: n! is the number of non-repetitive lists (permutations) of length n from n distinct symbols; defined by 0! = 1 and for n > 0, n! = n·(n−1)·(n−2)·...·2·1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factorial notation when counting permutations of all symbols. Motivating table and examples illustrate small n values (1,2,6,24,...).
